analysis.title: Given Inflation Risks, FOMC Minutes Point to Another Rate Hike Later This Year
key_insights: The FOMC voted unanimously at its September 15-16 meeting to raise the fed funds rate by 25 bps to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.
Participants saw the labor market as near full employment with some signs of strengthening, and said inflation remained elevated.
Most participants viewed risks as weighted toward higher inflation, and labor market risks as balanced.
Many participants viewed the September hike as insurance against inflation staying persistently above target due to stronger-than-expected demand or further adverse supply shocks.

Reasons given for the hike: protect against further unexpected inflationary pressures, slow inflation in the most likely outcome, keep inflation expectations from rising, and prevent strong AI demand from pushing inflation up further.
Several participants viewed policy as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive. Most participants judged another increase in the target range would likely be appropriate by year end.

Participants cited elevated core inflation and higher inflation from strong AI-related demand, while the inflationary impact of tariffs faded. Businesses were having more success passing higher input costs to customers.
Participants expected inflation to return to 2% in the medium term and expected labor market conditions to stay stable, with unemployment close to its current level.
Financial conditions were seen as supportive of growth despite the rise in longer-term Treasury yields, with equity prices up substantially this year and narrow corporate bond spreads.

Growth was described as solid, with robust business investment and resilient consumer spending. Several participants said underlying momentum appeared to have increased, and some said AI investment was surprising to the upside.
PNC forecasts no change at the October 27-28 meeting, a 25 bp hike in mid-December and another in mid-March, taking the fed funds rate to 4.25%-4.50% by early spring 2027.
